name: Vocabulary and Practice
title: Vocabulary and Practice
answer: Vocabulary practice is the area where technology has the strongest evidence for helping English learners, with adaptive tools and individualized software adding practice time that a single teacher cannot provide to every student. The gains are real but can fade, so teachers must plan review over weeks and months rather than days. Technology extends the teacher's work, it does not replace it.

sections.body: This idea concerns using technology to give English learners and newcomers more vocabulary and language practice than a classroom teacher alone can supply. Vocabulary is the area where the evidence for technology is strongest, and tools can adapt to each student's level while adding listening and speaking practice. The problem it solves is limited practice time: one teacher cannot give every student enough repetitions with the words they need. It also addresses the risk that short term vocabulary gains disappear without continued review. The practice must connect to the words students actually need for their classes, not to a separate word list.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, teachers use adaptive vocabulary tools such as Duolingo for Schools, which offers practice matched to the student and includes automatic child protections for younger users. The words practiced should come from the students' own class content so the practice supports their coursework. For listening, teachers can use text to speech tools to make audio versions of texts at different speeds, or record their own, and students can listen as many times as they need. Hearing academic language spoken helps students recognize it and eventually use it themselves. The text describes a randomized trial with middle school English learners, so individualized practice software is presented at that level, while the vocabulary trial with second graders and the study with first graders show the approach reaching younger students too.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels vocabulary as the area where the evidence for technology is strongest. It reports that meta analyses show large effects for technology assisted vocabulary learning across ages (Hao et al., 2021; Torres et al., 2025). It also reports a small study with first graders learning English as a foreign language in which AI generated picture cards beat paper cards on a test at the end of the unit, but the advantage disappeared on a later test (Temiz, 2025). A randomized trial with 221 middle school English learners in an urban district found that students who used individualized language practice software gained more in oral and listening skills than students in the regular curriculum alone (Harper et al., 2021). The book notes that short term gains can fade without continued practice.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Not every vocabulary gain lasts, as the first grade study shows, so teachers should plan review of words over weeks and months, not just days. The software adds practice time but the teacher still teaches, and the software only extends that practice. Tools must be chosen with care for younger students, which is why the text notes that Duolingo allows younger students with automatic child protections. The words practiced should connect to what students need for their classes rather than standing apart from the curriculum. The decisions about which words to teach, how to review them and how to fit practice into the school day remain with the teacher.
